newsitem.title: UK: Full text of February 5 UK monetary minutes.
newsitem.headline: Full text of February 5 UK monetary minutes.

text.p: The following is the complete text of the minutes of the February 5 monthly monetary policy meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George.
The Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Governor of the Bank of England met, together with officials, on 5 February, to review monetary developments.
Monetary and Economic Developments

2. Latest monetary and economic data (reviewed by officials before the meeting) provided further evidence that cost pressures remained weak, although the exchange rate had been more stable. There were continuing signs that activity remained strong, although more forward-looking indicators of business confidence and consumer demand were mixed.
Inflation Indicators

3. Underlying inflation (RPI excluding mortgage interest payments - RPIX) fell as expected, by 0.2 percentage points in December, to 3.1 per cent. This was due largely to a fall in used car prices and a smaller rise in petrol prices than in December 1995. All-items RPI inflation also fell by 0.2 percentage points, to 2.5 per cent.
4. Most other indicators confirmed that cost pressures remained weak:
-- sterling non-oil commodity prices were little changed in December, although they were 5.8 per cent lower than a year ago. The oil price had fallen back further to $22.6 per barrel;
-- sterling's effective exchange rate index had fallen back initially by over 1 percent, from 96.0 before the last meeting, before rising again, to 96.1 currently;

-- total non-oil import prices fell by 0.2 per cent in the three months to November compared to the previous three months, and were 0.3 per cent lower than a year ago. Non-EU import prices fell by 3.0 per cent in the three months to December on the previous three months;
-- the CIPS survey input price indicator fell again in January, as did the CBI survey output price expectations balance.
Monetary and Financial Indicators
5. Notes and coin grew by 0.8 per cent in January, up from 0.4 per cent in December; and the annual growth rate rose slightly, to 7.3 per cent. M0's annual growth rate rose to 7.4 per cent.

6. M4 fell by 0.2 per cent in December, following a rise of 1.1 per cent in November. The annual growth rate of M4 and M4 lending fell, to 9.6 per cent, and 8.3 per cent, respectively. However, these falls were related to sharp reductions in gilt repo activity at the year-end.

7. The Halifax house price index fell by 0.6 per cent in January, and the annual rate declined to 7.1 per cent. In contrast, the Nationwide index rose by 0.7 per cent in January, but the annual rate fell back to 8.2 per cent. Housing market transactions continued to grow strongly; in the three months to December particulars delivered (which lag actual transactions) were 12.3 per cent up on the previous three months, and 30.9 per cent higher than a year earlier.

8. Short-term interest rates were little changed in the US, Germany and Japan since the last meeting. UK short-term interest rates had fallen by around 10 basis points; and forward rates implicit in short-sterling futures contracts had fallen (by at least 20 basis points) at all maturities.

9. 10-year bond yields had fallen slightly (by 5 to 10 basis points) in the US, Germany and Japan. In the UK, yields on conventional gilts had fallen at all maturities (by up to 20 basis points). Since the last meeting inflation expectations implied by the gilt yield curve (calculated by the Bank from the difference between the yields on conventional and index-linked bonds) had fallen by around 20 basis points for both 5 years ahead and 10 years ahead.
Activity Indicators

10. In the US the preliminary estimate of GDP growth in 1996Q4 was stronger than expected at 1.2 per cent (not annualised), following growth of 0.5 per cent in Q3, leaving it 2.5 per cent up on a year earlier. Industrial production rose by 0.7 per cent in December, following a rise of 0.8 per cent in November. In Japan industrial production rose by 0.3 per cent in December, following a fall of 1.4 per cent in November.

11. In Germany the provisional estimate of 1996 GDP growth was 1.4 per cent, implying a slight fall in Q4. But industrial production rose by 1.4 per cent in December, following a rise of 0.9 per cent in November. Unemployment rose again in December to a new high of 10.9 per cent. In France unemployment also rose to a new high, of 12.7 per cent in November.

12. The preliminary estimate of UK GDP growth in Q4 showed that whole economy and non-oil GDP grew by 0.8 per cent and 0.7 per cent respectively, and were respectively 2.6 per cent and 2.5 per cent higher than a year earlier. Service sector output rose by 0.9 per cent, and was 3.4 per cent higher than a year ago.
13. Most other activity data were consistent with output growth continuing above trend, although indicators of business confidence and consumer demand were more mixed:

-- the BCC survey for Q4 implied strong growth in services, but less buoyant growth in manufacturing. This weaker result for manufacturing was backed up by the CBI survey which showed weaker output and orders, although the indicators remained above their long-run averages. However the January CIPS survey showed a rise in output and new orders indicators for manufacturing;

-- retail sales volumes fell by 0.8 per cent in December; but in the latest three months they rose by 0.9 per cent compared to the previous three months, and were 3.6 per cent higher than a year earlier;
-- consumer confidence rose in January to its highest level for over 8 years.
Summary of discussion

14. The Governor said that because it was just 3 weeks since the last meeting, there were fewer new data than usual, and what there were had been mixed. But, trying to abstract from the statistical "noise", the underlying trends were much as before. Output growth overall was picking up gradually, and was above trend - driven mainly by consumer demand. Net external trade was, on the other hand, probably currently being adversely affected by the strong exchange rate, restraining the growth of manufacturing output. Underlying monetary growth was still unsustainably strong. And although retail price inflation might be beginning to moderate as had been expected, and would be reduced in the near term by sterling's appreciation, the Bank still thought the odds were against meeting the inflation target of 2 per cent or less for RPIX two years ahead.

15. The main news on output had been the first estimate for Q4 GDP growth, which had ticked up further to 0.8 per cent - though it remained at 0.7 per cent excluding oil. Services output had risen by 0.9 per cent. And manufacturing output had continued to grow by 0.6 per cent in Q4 (as it had in Q3). All of these rates were above trend.

16. The Governor noted that, from the expenditure side, retail sales volume had fallen, by 0.8 per cent in the month of December, but that had still left it 0.9 per cent up in Q4 as a whole (compared with Q3). This was consistent with continuing above-trend growth of consumption as a whole of around 4 per cent a year. The year-on-year growth of both personal sector holdings of broad money (M4) and personal sector borrowing had picked up in Q4 as a whole; and although narrow money growth (notes and coin) had weakened in December, it increased strongly (by 0.8 per cent) in January, leaving year-on-year growth at 7.3 per cent. By comparison with the survey evidence available at the time of the last meeting (BRC and CBI Distributive Trades) - which related more specifically to the retail sector - the more recent surveys (BCC, CBI Quarterly Trends and CIPS) were more positive about domestic demand; and consumer confidence (from the GFK survey) recovered in January. In the housing market Halifax house prices fell back (down by 0.6 per cent) in January after their sharp (1.1 per cent) rise in December; but housing market turnover continued to increase on the latest figures (December).

17. Against this, external demand was clearly weakening. Excluding oil and erratics, export volumes had fallen by 2.4 per cent in November, and exports to non-EU countries by 9 per cent in December. And the surveys (BCC and CBI - though not CIPS) pointed to weaker manufacturing export prospects. Even so business optimism overall in manufacturing was holding up reasonably well on the back of domestic orders.

18. The Governor had already commented on narrow money growth. Broad money (M4) had actually fallen in December (by 0.3 per cent), as had total M4 lending (down by 0.6 per cent). But these developments had been more than accounted for by an over-the-end-year contraction of gilt-repo and reverse-repo business. Excluding this the underlying twelve-month growth rates for M4 and M4 lending were around 9 per cent and 8 per cent respectively - close to where they had been for well over the past year. The Bank's concern - as explained last month - was not that monetary growth was currently accelerating; it was the persistence of its unsustainably rapid rate of growth.

19. There were no new data on producer prices, but import prices (non-oil) had fallen by 2.9 per cent in November - the first significant fall since sterling began to appreciate. And non-EU import prices had fallen by around 4 per cent between August and December, during which time sterling had risen by over 10 per cent. There was therefore now clear evidence of a price effect of sterling's appreciation which should be increasingly reflected in lower goods price inflation at the retail level. Evidence of that happening so far was limited: prices of audio-visual equipment and toys had fallen slightly in December, which was unusual; and food prices had fallen by 2.2 per cent since August (though this might also reflect the good harvests in the UK). Annual RPIX inflation had nevertheless fallen in December (to 3.1 per cent, from 3.3 per cent in November) largely as a result of a drop in used-car prices and a smaller rise in petrol prices than in December 1995. Prices of consumer durables, and service sector prices, continued to rise, consistent with strong domestic demand in these sectors. Notwithstanding these upwards pressures, the Bank expected RPIX inflation to continue to fall through this year, under the impact of the exchange rate. But this effect was, as the Bank had said before, a one-off effect on the level of prices, rather than a continuing effect on the rate of inflation, which, into next year, would be determined by the rate of growth of overall demand.

20. The Governor said that none of this really changed the picture as seen to be evolving over the past few months. The Bank was not arguing - and had not argued - that the economy was accelerating out of hand. What the Bank had said was that it had been picking up steadily to a pace that could not be sustained for long consistently with the inflation target two years ahead. That remained the Bank's view. The rise in the exchange rate had improved the short-term prospect for inflation, and, if sustained, it would ease aggregate demand pressure through its effect on the net trade position. The Bank had allowed for both these effects in its forecasts, and in its policy advice. It, of course, recognised the problem for exporters. But domestic demand growth - particularly the growth of consumer spending - was already above the rate at which it could be sustained; and notwithstanding the "noise" in some of the recent data - including both the data on retail sales volumes and the monetary data for December - the signs were that it would persist at that rate. The Bank continued to advise that, to have a reasonable chance of hitting the inflation target two years ahead, the Chancellor needed to begin to take action now to moderate the pace of domestic demand growth by raising interest rates by per cent.

21. The Chancellor said there had not been much new data since the previous meeting, three weeks before. The new data that had been received had not caused him to change his mind - they showed a strong, healthy recovery that was sustainable. He saw no signs of inflationary pressures yet at a level which required action to be taken. In his view, the economy was on course to meet the inflation target two years out.

22. The Chancellor said that at the time of the last meeting he had wanted to wait to see the fourth quarter GDP figures. Although they were only the first, provisional estimates, they represented the most comprehensive measure of activity and put the current discussion into context. So far, the arguments in favour of raising interest rates now had been based on the view that the recovery was accelerating. The GDP figures had shown non-oil GDP growth at 0.7 per cent in the fourth quarter, under 3 per cent on an annualised basis. These figures did not support the views of some people that the economy had been growing unsustainably quickly.

23. The Chancellor said he was ready to step in when and if the economy did begin to grow unsustainably fast. But, in his view, the other data for December also confirmed a picture of healthy, steady growth. The CBI Survey was showing a sustainable level of activity. The CIPS Survey was a little more optimistic. But it was also evident from the surveys that the strength of sterling was already beginning to affect export demand, and this influence was likely to continue to be felt for some time.

24. The Chancellor said that the retail sales figures had confirmed some cooling off in consumer demand in December. After some strengthening in November, retail sales had fallen sharply, by 0.8 per cent, in December, and in the fourth quarter they were up 3.6 per cent on a year earlier.

25. The housing market was still recovering strongly. The Chancellor said he did not think that growth in house prices of 7-8 per cent a year was likely to persist for too long, and it was not at the moment alarming after six years of very depressed prices. With strong housing starts and more houses coming back onto the market, he expected house price inflation to ease off. He also noted that the Halifax house price index had actually fallen in January.

26. The Chancellor said that the producer price figures remained spectacularly good. And it was very encouraging that, despite the strength of the recovery, pay settlements remained subdued and there had been no acceleration of earnings. He felt that the Government's supply side policies to make the labour market more flexible had created a favourable climate, where the labour market could begin to tighten without feeding straight through into higher earnings growth.
27. M4 growth was still strong and M0 growth had accelerated marginally in January. They both continued to grow outside their monitoring ranges as they had done for some time.

28. The Chancellor said that the pound was around 15 per cent higher than a year ago, and that still concerned him. The markets had taken the rise in interest rates in October as a signal that there would be a rapid increase in rates, and this had reinforced the surge in the pound. There were signs that, as interest rate expectations had fallen back somewhat, the pound had steadied, albeit at a very much higher rate. But this was still likely to affect export performance, with knock-on effects on activity. It had also already had an impact on import prices and manufacturers' input costs.
29. The Chancellor agreed with the Governor that exchange rate movements should not be allowed to govern monetary policy, but they could not be ignored either.
30. In discussion the following points were made:

-- although the latest activity indicators suggested that growth was not accelerating, the cumulative picture over several months suggested the economy was growing above trend. There was also a possibility that GDP estimates would be revised upwards, as had tended to happen in periods of strong growth;

-- the recovery was uneven. Manufacturing growth had been relatively flat, and would be affected disproportionately by the strength of sterling, if it persisted. But services output had been growing strongly, and surveys suggested that capacity utilisation in services was at high levels and rising. The target measure for inflation - retail prices - included a significant element of services prices;

-- longer-term leading indicators of inflation - in particular broad money and house prices - had been rising strongly for some time. Although M4 had been affected by gilt repo transactions and house prices were still at relatively low levels, these indicators would suggest that inflation would start to pick up in the longer term;

-- however, there had been significant supply-side changes to the economy, which would allow the economy to grow faster without generating inflation pressures. Also the effects of the recession meant that consumers were still cautious, and earnings were restrained. This suggested that people were becoming accustomed to a low-inflation environment;

-- the exchange rate had appreciated since the summer by far more than had been expected. Although no significant effect had been seen yet, this would be expected to reduce inflation in the short term through a direct effect on retail prices, and in the longer term as demand was affected. However, the main effect would probably be to reduce the price level. And if inflation was to average 2 per cent or less, there would be periods when favourable shocks to inflation such as the higher exchange rate would take the inflation rate temporarily below 2 per cent.
